title: How much is it?
goal: Shop at the weekly market, ask about prices, use plurals, and count to a thousand.
bekal: form plurals for all three genders
tell Πόσο κάνει from Πόσο κάνουν
give prices per kilo and ask for change
count from a hundred to a thousand
name the most common fruit and vegetables

dialogs.title: ΔΙΑΛΟΓΟΣ — At the ΛΑΪΚΗ, the weekly market
dialogs.intro: Every neighborhood in Athens has a λαϊκή αγορά once a week: a whole street of fruit and vegetable stalls, much cheaper than the supermarket. Ana goes there on Tuesday morning. Notice that the verb changes too once the noun is plural.

lines.speaker: Πωλητής:
lines.id: Come on, come on! Fresh tomatoes!

lines.speaker: Άννα:
lines.id: Good morning. How much are the tomatoes?

lines.speaker: Πωλητής:
lines.id: Two euros a kilo. How much would you like?
lines.literal: two — euros — the — kilo. how-many (neut. pl.) — you-want?

lines.speaker: Άννα:
lines.id: A kilo, please. And the oranges?
lines.literal: one — kilo, please. and — the (neut. pl.) — oranges?

lines.speaker: Πωλητής:
lines.id: One fifty a kilo. They're from Crete.
lines.literal: one-and-a-half — euros — the — kilo. they-are — from — the — Crete.

lines.speaker: Άννα:
lines.id: Two kilos, then. How much is that all together?
lines.literal: two — kilos — then. how-much — they-make — all — together?

lines.speaker: Πωλητής:
lines.id: And five change. Thank you, dear!
lines.literal: and — five — change. I-thank, girl — my!

lines.speaker: Πωλητής:
lines.id: At the market it always is! Have a nice day!
lines.literal: in-the — people's-market — always! good — to-you — day!

notes: ⚠️ **Πόσο κάνει; for one item, Πόσο κάνουν; for several.** The verb goes plural along with the noun, just like "is / are" in English. Saying *Πόσο κάνει οι ντομάτες;* sounds as wrong to a Greek ear as "how much is the tomatoes?" does to yours.

**Prices per unit use the article, not a word for "per".** *Δύο ευρώ **το** κιλό* — literally "two euros the kilo". Likewise *πέντε ευρώ το άτομο* (five euros per person), *δέκα ευρώ η ώρα* (ten euros an hour).

**Ενάμισι = 1.5.** It's ένα + μισό fused together, and it changes with gender: **ενάμισι** κιλό (neuter), **ενάμισης** μήνας (masculine), **μιάμιση** ώρα (feminine). These three forms are heard often and rarely taught.

**Ρέστα (*REH-stah*) = change**, always neuter plural. *Κρατήστε τα ρέστα* means "keep the change" — in Greece a phrase for taxis rather than restaurants, since in restaurants the tip is left on the table.

**Κοπέλα μου, παιδί μου, αγόρι μου** — "my girl", "my child", "my boy" — are used by vendors, taxi drivers, and neighbors to anyone younger. ⚠️ This is **neither** flirting nor condescending; it's a close cousin of "love", "dear", or "honey" in British and American shop talk. Reacting stiffly is what would feel odd.
**Φρέσκος becomes φρέσκες in the feminine plural** and **φρέσκα** in the neuter plural. Adjectives go plural just as they follow gender — no new rule, just a slightly wider table.

**Λαϊκή αγορά literally means "people's market"**, from λαός (people) — the same word that gave English *laity* and *layman*. Each neighborhood has its own day, and prices in the last hour before closing can drop by half.

**Ακριβώς means "exactly"** — and ⚠️ don't confuse it with **ακριβός**, which means "expensive". They differ by a single letter: *ah-kree-VOHS* for both, but the spelling and use differ. Context always comes to the rescue.

grammars.title: Plurals: eight patterns, all predictable
body: If you know the singular ending, you know the plural ending. There are no irregular plurals to memorize at A1.
after: ⚠️ The **fem. -η** row is the only real surprise: η πόλη → **οι πόλεις**, not *οι πόλες*. The group is small but full of common words: πόλη (city), λέξη (word), τάξη (class), σκέψη (thought), δύναμη (strength). Learn those five and the rest can wait.
There are only three plural articles: **οι** for masculine and feminine, **τα** for neuter. In the object form: **τους / τις / τα**.

grammars.title: A hundred to a thousand
body: Hundreds are formed from the unit number plus -κόσια. The only thing to watch is that hundreds **change with gender**, unlike the teens and tens.
after: ⚠️ **101 isn't εκατό ένα but εκατόν ένα** — εκατό grows a -ν when another number follows. It's the only surprise in the whole Greek number system.
Years are said in full like ordinary numbers: 2026 = **δύο χιλιάδες είκοσι έξι** (two thousand twenty-six).

blocks.title: Phrases to use at the market stall
items: **Πόσο κάνει;** / **Πόσο κάνουν;** — How much is it? / How much are they?
**Ένα κιλό, παρακαλώ.** — A kilo, please. · **Μισό κιλό** — half a kilo. · **Δύο κιλά** — two kilos.
**Είναι φρέσκα;** — Are they fresh? · **Από πού είναι;** — Where are they from? Vendors at the λαϊκή love being asked this.

**Είναι λίγο ακριβό.** — It's a bit expensive. ⚠️ Haggling isn't the custom at the λαϊκή; what is customary is the **bonus**: vendors often throw in an extra handful or round the price down on their own.
**Τίποτα άλλο;** — Anything else? The answer is **Όχι, αυτά.** — No, that's all.
